references.text: The immediate context: James and John wanted to call down fire from heaven on the Samaritans, and Jesus turned to them and rebuked them.
Jesus weeps over Jerusalem instead of wishing destruction upon the city, which shows his attitude toward those who reject him – mercy rather than judgment.
Jesus rebukes (ἐπετίμησεν) Peter when he acted contrary to God's will, just as he rebukes the disciples here for their vengeful attitude.
Jesus teaches that one must love enemies and pray for those who persecute you – the opposite of calling down fire on those who reject you.
Jesus urges us to love enemies and be merciful, just as the Father is merciful – a fundamental attitude that contrasts with the disciples' desire to punish the Samaritans.
God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him – Jesus' rebuke of the disciples reflects this purpose.
God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but desires that he turn and live – this is the attitude Jesus shows when he rebukes the disciples' wish to destroy.
The following verse expands on the rebuke: The Son of Man has not come to destroy people's lives, but to save them.
The Lord's servant must not quarrel, but be kind to everyone, and in gentleness correct those who oppose – an attitude that reflects Jesus' rebuke of the disciples.
